headline.main: "Our Children Are Dying Before Our Eyes": Israel Is Starving the Gaza Strip
headline.social: "Our Children Are Dying Before Our Eyes": Israel Is Starving the Gaza Strip

intro: Experts have long been predicting a famine in the Gaza Strip. It has now arrived. The population is desperately trying to find food - but there is very little available. And people are dying.
text:
Sanaa was quite healthy early on, says her mother Suad al-Lahham, 30. But then, when she turned six months old, there was a sudden change and her daughter began losing weight. "We went to all kinds of doctors, neurologists, orthopedic specialists, a center for undernourished children, but nothing helped,” the mother says over the phone. Recently, her daughter’s condition suddenly deteriorated. She began refusing food and no longer moved, cried or played. "We knew that she could die at any time,” says her mother. "But we still didn’t give up hope.”
Then, on July 17, Sanaa fell asleep and her body grew icy cold despite the heat, her mother relates, and her arms and legs became stiff. Her eyes, big and gray, opened wide. Sanaa died at the age of one year and four months. She weighed less than two kilograms.
Her mother cries over the phone as she tells the story, her voice cracking.
Suad al-Lahham says she doesn’t know if Sanaa had an additional ailment that may have contributed to her malnourishment since such medical examinations are no longer possible in Gaza. But it is highly likely that her life could have been saved if Israel allowed more food, medicine and medical equipment into the Gaza Strip.
Her three other daughters, aged between four and eight, are also suffering from the lack of food, says their mother. They cry all day long and constantly say: "We’re hungry.” The mother says that she only weighs 47 kilograms herself and can hardly walk. She frequently suffers from dizziness – and she is four-months pregnant.
"Our children are dying before our eyes,” says Suad al-Lahham. "The whole world is watching as we die slowly and quietly. What can we still say? We have said all there is to say and it has changed nothing. Nobody is listening.”
After 22 months of war, the situation in the Gaza Strip is more catastrophic than it has ever been. The Israeli army continues to push forward, and for the first time last Sunday, it declared parts of the city of Deir al-Balah as an evacuation zone. The city was the only larger population center that ground troops hadn’t yet entered. Once again, tens of thousands of people were displaced, including the Lahham family – to that point among the lucky few in the Gaza Strip who were still living in their own homes. On Sunday, they moved into a tent in Mawasi, a desolate, overcrowded area of sand dunes southwest of Deir al-Balah.
According to the United Nations, 88 percent of the Gaza Strip is now under the direct control of the Israeli military or have been designated evacuation zones. The 2 million people in Gaza have been packed together an area that is hardly larger than the Mitte district in Berlin, divided into three islands surrounded by Israeli troops.
It is a situation that has raised an urgent question: Is this still a war, a fight against the Hamas terror organization, which launched the brutal October 7, 2023, attack on Israel? Is the primary aim of this war that of freeing the 50 or so remaining Israeli hostages kidnapped by Hamas on that day, only 20 of whom are thought to still be alive? Or has the goal shifted to that of permanently destroying the livelihood of Palestinians in Gaza?
Israel’s government has announced its intention to shelter hundreds of thousands of people in a camp in the southern part of the Gaza Strip, with plans calling for them to be resettled in other countries on the long term. It has been presented as a humanitarian measure. In truth, though, it is a forced displacement of the civilian population – and, as such, a war crime, possibly even a crime against humanity. An increasing number of renowned international law experts have even begun calling it genocide, given the systematic destruction and starvation.
No hostages have been freed for quite some time and Hamas has largely been vanquished. Even high-ranking Israeli soldiers and politicians have been saying for months that almost all of Israel’s military aims have been achieved.
At the same time, negotiations over a ceasefire and the release of the hostages are making no progress. For the last several months, the most significant hurdle standing in the way of such negotiations has been the refusal of the Israeli government to make a commitment to ending the war, which is a key Hamas demand. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing extremist coalition partners have threatened to leave the government should he agree to such a deal. Many in Israel now believe that Netanyahu may be trying to drag out the negotiations until the parliamentary summer break at the end of July before then making a deal – and thus delaying new elections.
Meanwhile, Israel continues attacking targets in the Gaza Strip, with dozens of people being killed almost every day, most of them civilians. The total number of deaths since the beginning of the war has now risen to almost 60,000 people. Residential buildings and infrastructure are being systematically destroyed and aid workers are being prevented from providing assistance. The few, halfway functioning hospitals are facing collapse because they hardly have any medicines or medical equipment left, not to mention fuel for generating electricity. On top of all that, the residents of the Gaza Strip are being starved – and those who seek to access aid supplies must risk their lives to do so.
Gaza has become a hell that is impossible to escape. And even those who have managed to somehow make it through the last almost two years of war are now desperate.
For a long time, international criticism of Israel’s war in the Gaza Strip remained muted. Warnings were issued and appeals made, but little was actually done. European countries, in particular, looked to the U.S., hoping that President Joe Biden or his successor Donald Trump would find a solution. But something has changed in recent weeks. A majority of European Union member states are now insisting that the Association Agreement with Israel either be reexamined or suspended. A weapons embargo or even sanctions against members of the Israeli government are under consideration. It has primarily been the German government that has stood in the way of such steps in recent months.
Most recently, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas sought to ward off sanctions by negotiating measures between the EU and Israel to improve the humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip.
Those measures called on Israel to open more border crossings, allow more aid supplies and fuel into the Gaza Strip and make it easier for bakeries and charity kitchens to operate. The deal also called for greater protections for aid workers and the repair of electricity and water lines.
Almost two weeks later, it has become clear that Israel’s government has done none of the above. The EU has allowed itself to be deceived and strung along – and it was all foreseeable.
The situation is even worse than it was before, admits a UN diplomat, who has asked that his name not be published. "The day will come when we will all have to ask what responsibility we bear.” A European diplomat also expresses disgust at the ignorance displayed by Brussels: "Our reports about the situation in Gaza are ignored because they don’t match up with the narrative people want to hear. The self-deception is unfathomable.”
Criticism of Israel has lately grown more pointed. Just recently, 30 foreign ministers from countries in Europe as well as Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Japan published a joint statement in which they demanded an immediate end to hostilities. "The suffering of civilians in Gaza has reached new depths,” it reads. "We condemn the drip feeding of aid and the inhumane killing of civilians, including children, seeking to meet their most basic needs of water and food.” Germany was not among the signatories.
On Wednesday, over 100 international aid organizations published a call for the end of the war and of the humanitarian blockade, including Save the Children, Doctors Without Borders and the German aid group Welthungerhilfe.
"As the Israeli government’s siege starves the people of Gaza, aid workers are now joining the same food lines, risking being shot just to feed their families,” they wrote. "Humanitarian organizations are witnessing their own colleagues and partners waste away before their eyes.” The statement quotes an aid worker, who says: "Children tell their parents they want to go to heaven, because at least heaven has food.”
The humanitarian system "is being impeded, undermined and endangered,” said UN Secretary-General António Guterres at the beginning of the week. Jonathan Whittall, who heads the UN humanitarian coordination office in Gaza, said in June: "This is carnage,” and spoke of "weaponized hunger.” It is, he said, "a death sentence for people just trying to survive.” Last Sunday, Israel announced that Whittall’s visa would not be extended.
The Pope has also criticized the "indiscriminate use of force” in Gaza. And even Donald Trump’s spokeswoman allowed that the war has become "quite brutal,” adding that "the president never likes to see that.”
There have been repeated warnings of famine in the Gaza Strip – and it has now arrived. The consequences are brutal. According to the World Food Program (WFP), one out of three people in the war zone are going for days without food because of the lack of supplies. People have reported that there is basically nothing left to buy, and that malnourished and dehydrated people are collapsing everywhere. Hospital employees are also reportedly hardly able to do their jobs because of hunger. At the same time, people are forced to walk long distances in extreme heat just to find anything to eat.
By Wednesday, a total of at least 110 deaths from malnourishment had been reported, with 80 children among them. In just the three days leading up to Wednesday, 44 people apparently died. These statistics are from the health ministry in the Gaza Strip, which is under the control of Hamas. They cannot be verified, but local doctors have also confirmed numerous deaths connected to malnourishment.
According to the British surgeon Nick Maynard, who was on duty in the Nasser Hospital in Gaza until Wednesday, four babies have died of malnourishment in that facility alone in recent weeks. He says that they no longer have supplies of the necessary baby formula and have only been able to give them a nutrient-poor sugar solution. Doctors have told DER SPIEGEL that an international aid worker who was trying to bring milk powder into the Gaza Strip had the powder taken away by soldiers as she was crossing the border.
Malnourished children are at far greater risk of infections and recover more slowly from injuries, such as those suffered in airstrikes. Even if they don’t die, many will suffer lifelong mental and physical impairments.
If the humanitarian situation remains as catastrophic as it currently is, the number of starvation victims is likely to climb rapidly.
Since the beginning of the war almost two years ago, Israel has been severely restricting the amount of food and other vital supplies allowed into the Gaza Strip. Sometimes the flow is increased, sometimes it is decreased, but it is never enough. And in early March, Israel implemented a complete blockade. In late May, the so-called Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) began distributing aid, supported by the Israeli government with the intention of replacing the work of the UN in Gaza.
But the system is dysfunctional, with aid supplies only being distributed at four sites located within military zones under the control of the Israeli military. Opening times vary, and sometimes supplies are gone within just 15 minutes, which is why people frequently spend the night nearby. And it is also why chaos frequently ensues. Israeli soldiers and sometimes even private security personnel regularly fire into the crowds that are pushing their way toward the GHF distribution sites.
According to the Palestinian authorities in Gaza, more than 1,000 people have been killed since the end of May as they were trying to access aid goods. The vast majority of them were killed at or near GHF distribution sites, while others were shot in the vicinity of UN aid convoys. Even if individual incidents cannot be fully clarified, reports from international media outlets, forensic experts, doctors and aid organizations reveal a clear pattern: The vast majority of the deaths are caused by the Israeli army. DER SPIEGEL has also spoken with witnesses who have reported being shot at by Israeli soldiers .
Last Sunday saw the worst such incident yet. According to the Palestinians, more than 70 people were apparently killed when they attempted to loot a UN World Food Program convoy in northern Gaza after it had passed through the Zikim border crossing.
DER SPIEGEL is in possession of an account from a Palestinian who was there. He says he saw soldiers firing at people at close range from a tank. A boy next to him was hit in the face by a bullet, he says, and died before his eyes. He, himself, was able to hide with his son behind a mound of sand. They were able to get away safely, he says, empty handed, but alive. The man says it was the worst thing he has ever experienced.
"Hunger has made people so desperate that they just rush forward,” says a UN aid worker currently in the Gaza Strip.
He blames Israel. For one, because it is the Israeli blockade that has created the desperation that has led to the looting in the first place. And for another, he says, Israel has undermined all efforts to avoid such looting. Prior to the most recent shipment on Sunday, the UN aid worker says, the WFP made several requests to the Israeli army to keep their distance from the convoy to prevent yet another massacre. "In vain. The people rushed the convoy, and the Israelis fired on them.”
The WFP has also officially blamed Israeli tanks and snipers for the deadly gunfire. The Israeli army, by contrast, has claimed that it fired "warning shots” in response to a "threat.”
The Israeli army has made it impossible to secure the transports, says the UN aid worker. Early in the war, police forces formally under the control of Hamas provided effective security for aid deliveries, he says, but they were repeatedly targeted by Israeli forces. The Israeli leadership has also taken issue with local security personnel, he says. It seems, he says, as though there is a strategy behind it: "to completely hamstring the UN system so that only the GHF is left.”
Now that the humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip is once again in the international spotlight, Israeli officials have begun disseminating images purportedly showing 950 truckloads of aid supplies waiting to be picked up by aid workers. The message: There is no famine. And if there is, it is the UN’s fault.
But numbers provided by the Israelis themselves tell a different story: In the last two months, around 4,500 trucks full of aid supplies have been brought into the Gaza Strip. One half has gone to the GHF, the other to the UN and other aid organizations. That may sound like a lot, but it is an average of just 75 trucks per day. Prior to the war, around 600 trucks of supplies entered the Gaza Strip each day.
In addition, UN personnel have been complaining for months about being unable to pick up aid deliveries because of the Israeli army’s refusal to provide the authorization they need to cross the war zone. And almost everything that does get picked up is looted. "Self-distribution,” is the fatalistic term used at the UN to describe the situation. Now, aid workers are also facing the risk that dozens of those seeking access to aid will be killed by the Israeli army.
Israel, in short, has put the UN in an impossible position.
Solidifying that impression is the fact that the army on Sunday ordered the evacuation of parts of the city of Deir al-Balah – including areas where the UN and many humanitarian aid agencies have their headquarters. Several warehouses are located there as well, along with provisional clinics, three wells and a desalination plant. The water from the desalination plant supplies hundreds of thousands of displaced people in Mawasi. It is currently unclear whether it will continue to flow.
And the UN has also been directly targeted. On Sunday evening, Israel attacked the World Health Organization’s (WHO) central warehouse, with an artillery shell reportedly blowing a hole in the roof before a quadcopter – an armed drone – then apparently flew in through the hole and destroyed a generator. After a fire broke out, warehouse guards pulled back, whereupon people from a refugee camp across from the warehouse plundered the building.
DER SPIEGEL on Monday was able to speak to a UN aid worker at the site. "I can see tanks,” he said. During the conversation, gunfire could constantly be heard along with the occasional explosion. "I can see civilians who are looting everything they can get their hands on: cleaning supplies, batteries, pots, food.”
On Monday, a WHO residential building, allegedly with at least 30 personnel and their family members inside, was attacked in the same way. Following an initial artillery salvo, a quadcopter allegedly triggered a fire. Meanwhile, the army apparently surrounded the building, with Israeli soldiers sending women and children through the war zone towards Mawasi and handcuffing and searching the men. The soldiers took one of them away, and it is unknown what has become of him. Afterwards, several tanks allegedly inflicted significant damage to the building and vehicles belonging to the WHO, which had been prepared for evacuation, were destroyed.
It is unclear how aid workers should continue their work, says the UN aid worker. "We will have to see how much of our quarters, our stockpiles, our vehicles and our material remains.” The stockpiles contained medical supplies, medicines and other urgently needed items intended for hospitals in Gaza.
Following the attack, the WHO spoke of a "pattern of systematic destruction of health facilities.” The group’s "operational presence” in Gaza was now "compromised, crippling efforts to sustain a collapsing health system and pushing survival further out of reach for more than 2 million people.”
More than 90 percent of all hospitals in the Gaza Strip have been damaged or destroyed by Israel since the beginning of the war, with the WHO counting a total of far more than 600 attacks on healthcare facilities. Upwards of 1,500 medical workers have been killed, according to the Health Ministry in Gaza. Dozens have been arrested by the Israeli army, with many still in captivity several months later. Some of those who have been released say they were tortured.
The Israeli destruction of hospitals and medical equipment has been particularly notable in northern Gaza. A modern dialysis center was torn down by Israeli bulldozers while a clinic specializing in cancer treatment, which had only been opened just a few years earlier in central Gaza, was initially occupied by the Israeli army before then being blown up.
Now, Israel is directly targeting aid workers, the last people who still have the ability to bring medicines and food into the Gaza Strip. If the WHO and other UN organizations lose their ability to operate in the Gaza Strip, only the GHF distribution sites would remain. And that would be a disaster for the people of Gaza.
"We no longer know what to do,” says Heba Abdel Dayem, 39, close to tears. Her husband is one of the several thousand people to have been injured in the last two months while trying to obtain aid supplies. On June 23, he was hoping to get his hands on a bit of flour for his family from a UN convoy that had entered the Gaza Strip through the Zikim border crossing. But on this day, too, Israeli soldiers fired into the crowd. Mohammed Abdel Dayem, a former taxi driver who had been unemployed since the start of the war, was hit in the head by a bullet.
Since then, the right side of his body has been largely paralyzed and he is unable to talk. He is also malnourished and has dark rings under his eyes. He lies listlessly on a thin mattress in a tent in Gaza City, his urine fed through a tube into a plastic bag lying on the floor in front of him.
The family has been displaced 10 times during the war, says Heba Abel Dayem. Their tent has grown worn and hardly offers any protection anymore, but they are unable to find a new one. For the last four months, Israel has no longer been allowing tent material or tarps into Gaza.
Abdel Dayem’s seriously injured husband needs medical care and drugs, but she currently has no access to either. On top of that, she says, their youngest child Mohammed is sick, suffering from a shortage of blood platelets. He is in need of healthy food, fruit, vegetables and meat – but the family has had none of that for months, she says.
They had nothing at all to eat on the previous day, she says, and were only able to buy chickpeas on this day – one kilogram for 80 shekels, the equivalent of 20 euros. Usually, they drink water during the day to calm their pangs of hunger, says Abdel Dayem. They haven’t had any backup supplies for quite some time, only just scraping together enough to survive. On a small table in the tent, there are a few spices, a half-empty bottle of cooking oil and a can of beans.
She has frequent bouts of dizziness because of hunger, she says, and has wounds on her body that are likely the result of the poor hygienic conditions in which they are forced to live in combination with a weakened immune system. Plus, she cleans her clothes with improvised detergent that produces skin irritation.
"It is a terrible feeling to see your child crying for food and be unable to give him anything,” says Heba Abdel Dayem. "The feeling of helplessness is unbearable. Only those who have gone through it themselves can understand it.” She has just managed to purchase a tiny piece of bread for her injured husband. It cost the equivalent of around two euros, she says.
Vendor Mohammed al-Khodari, 22, confirms the widespread lack of food. "The markets are empty,” he says. At his simple stand in Gaza City, he sells items that usually come from GHF centers. People offer him looted food, he says, to obtain money for other things they badly need. Israel has claimed that the establishment of the GHF distribution sites put a stop to the trade in aid goods, from which Hamas is also allegedly profiting. But that isn’t the case.
Some things simply aren’t available at all anymore. "Flour can no longer be found, and it is difficult to find rice,” says Khodari. He claims that he charges only a small markup on food, earning just one euro on a kilogram of rice that he sells for the equivalent of 20 euros. He says that customers often berate him for the high prices. But it’s not his fault, he insists – he is barely getting by himself.
"The international community has made a lot of promises,” he says. "Here in Gaza, we have seen nothing. Nothing has arrived and the situation has only grown worse.”
Vital for the survival of many people in Gaza are the charity kitchens, known as Takiya. But many of them have had to cease operations in recent weeks and months. Most recently, the U.S. aid organization World Central Kitchen announced on Sunday that it had to shut down for the second time this year. The organization distributed 80,000 meals on the day before the announcement, but said its stockpiles were now exhausted – despite the fact, the organization noted, that fully loaded trucks on the other side of the border were waiting to cross into Gaza.
Jamal Subh operates a charity kitchen in Gaza City. The restaurant he owned was destroyed in the war and he now cooks meals for the needy in the courtyard of a different restaurant, also now closed. Huge pots sit on stones over an open fire. The food and money he needs to operate the kitchen comes from aid organizations. He and his 20 co-workers begin cooking at dawn and finish by 10 a.m. Then, vehicles from the aid organizations show up and bring the pots to emergency housing facilities and refugee camps.
"The ingredients we are currently using are from stockpiles that we were able to amass during the last ceasefire, but they are now almost completely used up,” says the cook. A few months ago, they were still able to prepare rice, beans, peas and noodles. Now, they almost exclusively make lentils, he says, adding that he pays more than the equivalent of 20 euros per kilogram. "It’s crazy,” he says. "The only thing left to buy are legumes. But even those, most people can’t afford.”
Beyond food itself, their biggest problem is gas and other fuels, Subh says. There is hardly any firewood anymore, and they use whatever they can find in the ruins of destroyed homes, he says. Bedframes, wardrobes, water tanks, clothes – anything that burns.
On this Saturday afternoon, Subh and his co-workers are busy washing pots and chopping wood.
"Often, children show up barefoot in tattered clothes, faces smeared with dirt,” he says. "They are carrying empty containers and ask us for food, but we can’t give them anything. Our job is to cook, not to distribute.”
It breaks his heart to see these children, he says. "They should be in school, not on the streets searching for food! They’ve been robbed of the best time of their lives: their childhood.”
